source: Campitelli and Gobet (2004) Adaptive expert decision making: skilled chess players search more and deeper (ICGA Journal 27(4))
finding: Full text now read (the earlier Cloudflare block was on another host). Four players, three hard positions needing 52, 60 and 70 nodes and 23, 25 and 35 plies. Search depth, rate and node count rise linearly with Elo. Top players searched 2 to 10 times more than in the de Groot, Saariluoma and Gobet studies.
numbers: GM 2550, IM 2500, CM 2100, class B 1750 (one player each; class B lost position C). Mean depth 13.8/10.5/7.4/2.8 plies; max depth 25/23.7/17.7/10.5; nodes 370/405/152.7/88; rate 12.3/13.5/6.8/3.2 nodes per min; move quality 4.3/4.7/3.0/3.0 (IM above GM). Mean depth = -18.3 + 0.012 x Elo, r(4)=.97, p<.02 one-tailed (2.4 plies per 200 Elo). Max depth = -19.9 + 0.018 x Elo, r=.99 (3.6 plies per 200 Elo). Nodes = -645 + 0.4 x Elo. Earlier top players: mean depth 5.4 (de Groot), 3.6 (Saariluoma), 5 (Gobet); nodes 35, 23, 58. 30 min limit per position.
quote: previous research has vastly underestimated experts' search potential
limits: N=4, one player per level, so the regression has 4 points and the p values are one-tailed. Players were young (21 and 22). Positions B and C told players to find a unique solution, which differs from de Groot's instruction and may itself push search. No easy position was run in the same think-aloud task. The authors say the sample is too small for precise estimates.
agent_relevance: Confirms the numbers behind K04: 2.4 plies per 200 Elo is correct but comes from 4 people. Depth budget should follow how deep the task needs, not a fixed expert-like number.

source: Campitelli and Gobet (2004), qualitative section and supplementary tasks
finding: The same four players differed in how they ran the search. CM and class B made no candidate list and jumped between moves. The GM also jumped, but kept and extended a candidate list and knew he was undisciplined. The IM followed Kotov: a list, rarely changed, each move analysed to an evaluation. Both IM and GM had read Kotov. In fast tasks the skill gradient stayed.
numbers: 10 s decisions on 49 positions (about 10.4 nodes, 6.4 plies): GM 23 solved (46.9%), IM 18 (36.9%), CM 4 (8.2%), class B 2 (4.1%); r=.94. 5 s recall of game positions 83.2/85/54/47%; random positions 21.7/19/17.7/15.5%. Cumulative study hours 6890/7904/1872/416.
limits: Single players, no outcome comparison of disciplined versus jumping search. The most disciplined player (IM) had the best move quality by a small margin (4.7 vs GM 4.3), which is one data point and not a test. Authors conclude search behaviour is not restricted to progressive deepening and can be under strategic control.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open for outcomes. This is the only human case where discipline and quality line up, and only for one IM. Revisit policy is a choice an agent can make, not a fixed property of expert search.

source: Connors, Burns and Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot (Cognitive Science 35(8))
finding: Abstract and record pages only (ECU repository, Macquarie page). Full text is paywalled (Wiley returned 403) and no open copy was found. A de Groot replication with 22 players on two positions. Stronger players search faster, and today's top players search much faster than players in earlier studies. The authors still say de Groot's main conclusion holds and fits pattern-recognition models.
numbers: 6 grandmasters, 5 international masters, 6 experts, 5 class A players; two positions; think-aloud. Abstract result: GMs and IMs search more quickly than experts and class A. No depth or node numbers were available.
limits: No depth numbers, so it can neither confirm nor deny the 2.4 plies per 200 Elo slope. The abstract stresses speed, not depth. Gap 8 stays open for this paper.
agent_relevance: The measured skill effect here is speed (nodes per minute), a throughput effect, not a depth-policy effect. For an LLM that maps to useful steps per token, not to deeper chains.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: Closest thing to a direct equal-compute test of revisiting. A PaLM 2-S* model fine-tuned to revise its earlier answers, with a verifier, was run two ways on MATH: N revisions in sequence versus N independent samples in parallel. Sequential narrowly won. The best mix of sequential and parallel depended on question difficulty: easy questions did best with all-sequential revisions, hard questions needed a balance with parallel sampling.
numbers: Same generation count N (budgets up to 256 generations). The compute-optimal split matched parallel best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (for example 64 vs 256 samples). The revision model turned about 38% of already-correct answers into wrong ones if used naively, so selection by majority vote or verifier over the chain is needed. Revision models were fine-tuned with up to 4 earlier wrong answers in context.
limits: Needs fine-tuning for revision (the paper says capability-specific fine-tuning is necessary). MATH only. A learned verifier does the selection. Compute is counted in generations, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Nearest thing to the gap 1 study. Revision is good for items the model is nearly right on, and a fresh independent start is better for hard ones. An S4/S5 rule should send hard items to a new path, not a longer edit of the old one.

source: Snell et al. (2024), difficulty estimation section
finding: Difficulty can be estimated and used to pick the strategy. Five bins per model, from pass rate over 2048 samples per question. A label-free version bins by the average verifier score of those same samples. The two give nearly the same compute-optimal curves. The paper does not count the cost of getting the estimate.
numbers: Model-defined bins predicted test-time compute efficacy better than the hand-labelled MATH difficulty levels. At the hardest level (5) almost no method helps, and extra pretraining beats extra test-time compute there. The estimate used 2048 samples per question, far more than the final budgets of 4 to 256 generations.
limits: Estimation cost is stated and left to future work. One model family, one task.
agent_relevance: Answers the second half of gap 3 only in part: a verifier-based difficulty signal works, but this version is expensive. See d12 for a version that needs 4 samples.

source: Snell et al. (2024), search against verifiers by difficulty
finding: Breadth and depth of search also depend on difficulty. Beam search beat best-of-N at small budgets and on hard questions (levels 3 and 4). On easy questions (levels 1 and 2) beam search got worse as budget grew, which the authors read as over-optimising the verifier. Lookahead search was usually worse than beam search at the same budget. On level 5 nothing helped.
numbers: Budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations. Lookahead cost counted as N x (k+1) samples.
limits: Process reward model on MATH. Search is over solution steps, not candidate first moves. The easy-problem harm comes from a learned verifier, so with an exact checker it may not appear.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 7: the best amount of search depends on difficulty, and on easy items more search with an imperfect judge does harm. Candidate width should shrink when the first answer is already well supported.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han and Zhang (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction of LLMs (arXiv 2406.01297 v3)
finding: Survey of self-correction work up to May 2024. Three conclusions: no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted LLM feedback alone except on tasks unusually suited to it; self-correction works well when reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Many papers use oracle labels, weak first prompts or weak baselines, which inflates results.
numbers: Survey, no single effect size. It gives a checklist: fair comparison to the best initial response and to strong baselines such as sampling several times.
limits: Cutoff May 2024, before most reasoning-model work. Table text extraction was garbled, so only the abstract-level conclusions were used. It runs no equal-token experiment of its own.
agent_relevance: Supports the working answer to gap 2: a revisit helps when it brings new information (a tool, a checker, retrieved knowledge, a different attempt) and not when it is only 'look again'. It also says to compare any revisit rule with plain resampling at equal cost.

source: Singh, Ghosal, Gharat, Pal, Narayanam and Manocha (2026) ThinkRetrieve: retrieval-augmented reasoning traces for test-time scaling (arXiv 2608.10928)
finding: The cleanest test so far of what makes a revisit useful. Plain forced 'Wait' continuation (sequential test-time scaling as in s1) stalled or fell as the thinking budget grew. Revisits that inject a retrieved solved example into the trace at each step kept improving. Random examples helped less than relevant ones. Examples given once up front, not per step, did little.
numbers: Five models (1.5B to 8B), GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025, 3 seeds, thinking budget up to 22,528 tokens with exemplar tokens counted against it. Table 1 (best accuracy across budgets), AIME 2025, Qwen3-1.7B: standard 24.4, sequential 22.2, static ICL 23.3, random retrieval 27.8, ThinkRetrieve 35.6 (+13.4 over the 22.2 sequential figure; text says sequential plateaus near 22%). DeepSeek-R1-1.5B GSM8K: sequential fell from 83% to 52% at 22K tokens while ThinkRetrieve stayed at 84%. Qwen3-32B MATH-500 peaked near 15K tokens and then fell. Generated tokens 12,913 vs 15,847 for sequential at the same budget. ThinkRetrieve wins every cell in the tables.
limits: Math only. A 310K-example synthetic NuminaMath corpus with a similarity filter at 0.90 (max retained 0.898), so near-duplicate problem classes remain. AIME has 30 problems. The table reports best accuracy over budgets, not accuracy at one budget. Preprint, one lab, not replicated. Random retrieval beat plain sequential in 3 of 5 AIME cells, so part of the gain is 'any injected content' and part is relevance.
agent_relevance: Strong support for the rule that a revisit should carry new information. It isolates the variable the gap asked for: same budget and mechanism, only the content of the re-entry changes (nothing, random, relevant).

source: Wu, Sachan, Yih and Chen (2026) Procedural knowledge at scale improves reasoning (Reasoning Memory, COLM 2026, arXiv 2604.01348)
finding: A memory of solved cases beats more search at a matched sampling budget. A 32-million-entry store of subquestion and subroutine pairs from earlier reasoning traces is queried inside the model's own thinking. Against a retrieval-free baseline that samples the same number of trajectories and filters by length, it won 34 of 36 comparisons.
numbers: Three models (R1-Distill-Llama-8B, OpenThinker3-7B, Qwen3-32B), six benchmarks, budgets (m,n)=(8,4) and (30,8) trajectories. Average over all models and tasks 0.580 vs 0.500 for no retrieval. Abstract: +19.5% over no retrieval and +8.9% over the compute-matched baseline at the higher budget. At m=30 gain over no retrieval 19.0% on math, 9.8% on science, 28.9% on coding. Document, full-trajectory and template retrieval mostly did not beat no retrieval.
limits: Matching is on the number of sampled trajectories, not total tokens, and retrieved text adds prompt tokens (cost table not read). The datastore comes from public reasoning corpora that may overlap benchmarks despite the authors' checks. Preprint-level for the cited numbers.
agent_relevance: First positive answer to gap 4 in LLMs: a case library can beat plain extra sampling. It matches the human pattern where Elo carries skill beyond search. The library must hold procedures, not whole past answers.

source: Chen, Koenig and Dilkina (2025) Iterative deepening sampling as efficient test-time scaling (arXiv 2502.05449)
finding: A direct LLM version of progressive deepening. Each sample gets a token budget that grows by a factor alpha each round. If a sample is not finished, a self-check trigger sentence is appended ('wait' for reasoning models) and the sample continues. A finished answer is not revisited. It beat vanilla sampling at equal wall-clock cost on MATH-500 and AIME.
numbers: MATH-500 and AIME-24/25, plotted against 'equivalent N' that charges the extra time. For weak models on AIME-24, ID-sampling at N=1 exceeded vanilla at N=32. Table 2 (a DeepSeek-R1-distill Qwen model on AIME-24): pass@1 72.6 vs 75.5, cons@32 83.3 vs 86.7. Relative wall-clock time 1.00 vanilla, 1.07 / 1.09 / 1.39 for alpha 2.5 / 2.0 / 1.5. Alpha 2.0 recommended. Majority voting did poorly with it for non-reasoning models.
limits: The Table 2 caption is ambiguous between a 7B and a 32B model in the text I read. A 3-point gain on 30 problems is within noise. Trigger text is model-specific ('wait' alone does not work on non-reasoning models). No variance reported. No verifier.
agent_relevance: A revisit schedule (early and often, then fading) that costs about 7 to 9% extra time. The rule 'do not revisit a finished answer' is a design choice the authors argue for but do not isolate with an ablation.

source: Mirtaheri, Edelman, Jelassi et al. (2025) Let me think! A long chain-of-thought can be worth exponentially many short ones (arXiv 2505.21825)
finding: Theory plus experiments on graph connectivity: at a fixed total token budget, one longer sequential chain beats many short parallel chains with a vote. This held for small transformers trained from scratch and for three reasoning models (Qwen3-32B, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, s1-32B). It takes about a thousand tokens of sequential reasoning before parallel voting helps at all.
numbers: Authors state that for a fixed total token budget, sequential scaling always beats parallel scaling on this task family. Parallel scaling only helps once sequential scaling has reached non-trivial accuracy. s1-32B on AIME2024 shows the same direction.
limits: Synthetic bridge graphs built so that depth is needed. Does not show sequential beats parallel in general. Snell finds parallel better on hard MATH items.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for gaps 1 and 3. Deepening in the same chain wins when the task has real serial depth. Independent restarts win when the first approach is the problem.

source: Nguyen, Gupta and Le (2026) Uncertainty-aware budget allocation for adaptive test-time reasoning (arXiv 2605.26849 v2)
finding: A cheap difficulty signal. Give every question 4 samples, measure how much the answers disagree (vote entropy), then spend the remaining fixed budget on the questions whose answers disagree. The first samples also count in the final vote. No extra model, no extra calls.
numbers: Five open-weight models, five benchmarks, default N=4 samples per question. Average +2.3% accuracy over uniform allocation, up to +5.5% (GSM8K, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.2-3B). Beat uniform in 14 of 15 settings in the main table; 9 of 15 improvements significant at p<0.05. Gains largest at N=4 to 8, and the gain was not largest at the hardest level.
limits: Needs answers that can be compared (short numeric or option answers). Gain is modest. Open-ended answers need another disagreement measure. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Answers the 'cheap enough' half of gap 3: disagreement among a few first passes is a usable difficulty estimate that costs nothing extra because the samples are reused. Fits a first pass that sets the depth budget.

source: Li et al. (2025) SelfBudgeter: adaptive token allocation for efficient LLM reasoning (arXiv 2505.11274)
finding: A model trained with reinforcement learning to predict its own token budget before reasoning. Budgets rise with problem difficulty across tiers, and length falls while accuracy stays or rises on easy sets. On the hardest set the 7B version lost accuracy.
numbers: 1.5B model: GSM8K 84.10% at 1,232 tokens (R1-Distill-1.5B 73.09% at 2,865); MATH500 78.47% at 2,327 (74.93% at 5,327); AIME2025 21.11% at 4,288 (22.22% at 14,444). 7B model: GSM8K 90.30 at 991; MATH500 86.87 at 2,667; AIME2025 6.67 at 12,242 (R1-Distill-7B 28.89 at 22,159, though that row in the garbled table is my pairing). Abstract: 61% average length compression on math.
limits: Needs training (cold start plus budget-guided GRPO). The AIME2025 7B row shows a drop, so the difficulty estimate may fail at the hard end, where it matters most. AIME has 30 problems. Table text was garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only scaffold cannot copy this, but it shows models can learn a fair difficulty-to-budget map and that it may fail on the hardest items. Argues for a budget floor when the first pass is uncertain.

source: Guan et al. (2026) Constructing Pareto frontiers of optimal reasoning termination methods for overthinking in reasoning models (OTBench, arXiv 2610.13570)
finding: Measures what stopping at the best point would give. For each reasoning trace, the answer is re-sampled from truncated prefixes to find the earliest prefix with top accuracy. Most thinking tokens come after that point, and full thinking is on average 9 points less accurate than that reference. The loss is concentrated in some tasks. Oracle per-trace stopping reaches full-thinking accuracy at a far lower budget than a fixed cap.
numbers: Six models (GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-4B and 30B-A3B Thinking, R1-Distill-Qwen 7B/14B/32B), AIME, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench; 70.5B reasoning tokens. Mean overthinking ratio (tokens after the best prefix) 64.3%; mean accuracy drop to full thinking 9.03 points. By task: MATH ratio 78.8% but drop 1.83; GPQA 61.4% but drop 16.98; LCB drop 12.42; AIME 4.88. Oracle budget cap needed to match full-thinking accuracy: 71.4% (route or not), 35.0% (fixed cap), 14.2% (dynamic early exit). Oracle ceilings about 73%, 76%, 81%.
limits: The reference prefix is chosen on the same noisy probes it is measured on, so the loss is biased upward (best-of-many selection). 16 trajectories per question. Frontiers are oracle upper bounds, not deployable methods. Truncation is fixed-prefix and re-answer, not a live agent.
agent_relevance: A measured answer for gap 9: keeping the best-scoring state beats taking the last one, but only a stopping signal the agent can see can capture it. For gap 10: accuracy is flat over much of the late budget on MATH but not on GPQA or code, so the budget curve is task-dependent, not one shape.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models (DEER, arXiv 2504.15895 v3)
finding: A training-free stopping rule. At step transition points the model is asked for a trial answer. If its confidence in that answer is high, thinking stops. About 75% of AIME24 samples contain a point where stopping early gives the correct answer, and some correct answers are reachable only by stopping early.
numbers: 11 reasoning models, 10 benchmarks. Chain length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average with accuracy up 0.3 to 5.0 points. In MATH-500 and GPQA, 60.8% and 35.1% of correctly answered samples keep their correctness after only 20% of the steps.
limits: The confidence signal is the model's own, so confident wrong answers end early. Ranges are across models and sets, not a single headline. The 75% figure is from AIME24 questions only.
agent_relevance: A usable stopping test for S5: stop on a trial answer held with high confidence, otherwise continue. Supports keeping the best-so-far answer at each transition rather than only the last one.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning (arXiv 2307.13702)
finding: Tests whether the written steps drive the answer by cutting them (early answering) or inserting a mistake (adding mistakes). Reliance on the chain varies hugely by task. On the three least reliant tasks the chain changes the final answer less than 10% of the time, and on the most reliant (AQuA) more than 60%. Larger models relied on the chain less (inverse scaling) on most tasks.
numbers: A 175B RLHF assistant, eight multiple-choice tasks, mean chain 4 steps (89% of chains 3 to 6 steps). Seven of eight tasks gain from chain of thought. Replacing the chain with filler tokens gave no accuracy gain. Generated mistakes were plausible at least 80% of the time by the authors' check.
limits: 2023 model, short chains, multiple choice. Measures reliance on the chain, not on a particular branch. Not a replication of the four-in-a-row 32.0% vs 1.2% ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports the design rule that the final answer should come from evaluated branches by code or an explicit citation step, since the written trace can be ignored. Reliance depends on task, so test it per task type.

source: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda and Conmy (2025/2026) Thought anchors: which LLM reasoning steps matter? (arXiv 2506.19143 v4)
finding: A resampling test of which sentences matter. For each sentence, 100 rollouts are run with it and 100 from a replacement, and the shift in final answers is measured. Planning sentences and uncertainty-management sentences (re-evaluation, backtracking) have the highest counterfactual effect, more than computation or fact retrieval. So some revisit sentences do steer the answer.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on MATH, 20 problems solved 25 to 75% of the time, one correct and one incorrect trace each (40 traces), mean 144.2 sentences and 4,208 tokens per trace. A second model (R1-Distill-Llama-8B) is in an appendix.
limits: Small set (20 problems), math only, one model in the main analysis. Measures sentence-level influence, not the branch-level ablation of the four-in-a-row study, so it is related evidence and not a replication.
agent_relevance: Partial support for gap 6 in math: backtracking and planning sentences are causally used. Resampling at a sentence can test whether a revisit step mattered, at about 100x the cost, so use cheap proxies in a scaffold.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility in clinical problem-solving (mARC, arXiv 2601.11866)
finding: Einstellung traps in medicine: 100 items built so that the familiar answer is wrong. Strong reasoning models at their highest reasoning effort matched physicians; non-reasoning models did poorly. On the 20 items most physicians missed, the best model was confidently right on 55%. This shows models can resist a trap but does not test a forced second pass.
numbers: Five physicians, mean accuracy 0.66 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.75). Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (CI 0.738 to 0.763), mean over 15 runs; no significant difference from physicians for it, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1 and Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning. Human-miss set (20 of 100 items, defined as a physician majority wrong): physicians 36% (CI 26 to 46) vs 73% on other items; best model 55.0% decisively correct [39.9, 80.0], 25.0% decisively wrong, 20.0% indeterminate.
limits: The miss set is defined from the same five physicians who set the human baseline, which inflates the gap by selection. Items were written by the same group. Reasoning effort and model change together, so it does not separate more tokens from a different mechanism. Medical QA, not a first-answer-then-better-answer task.
agent_relevance: For gap 5: higher reasoning effort already lowers fixation in strong models. No study tested 'exclude the first answer's key elements' as a forced second pass. The gap stays open and needs our own run.
